technical: Instructions and context supplied to a model to guide its response.
human: Ordering dinner: 'make food' is vague; 'chili pork, less salt, no ginger, plated for a photo' gives the cook a useful brief.
business: A clearer spec can reduce rework and review cycles; measure task success and revisions, not vibes.
caveat: A prompt cannot guarantee compliance or correctness.

technical: Software that uses a model to plan and invoke tools across multiple steps toward a goal.
human: A junior teammate with a checklist, access badge, tools and a supervisor—not a magical employee who can enter every room.
business: Automates bounded workflows; compare labor saved with supervision, API and exception-handling costs.
caveat: Needs permissions, tool outputs, observability and approval for risky actions.

technical: The maximum sequence of model input and output tokens available in one request or interaction.
human: A meeting table with limited space: once it's full, notes must be moved, summarized or removed.
business: Determines how much document/chat material fits; affects retrieval strategy and per-request spend.
caveat: Context capacity is not permanent memory or guaranteed recall.

technical: A documented interface through which software systems exchange requests and responses.
human: A standardized hotel reception desk: submit a known request format and get an agreed response.
business: Faster integrations versus rebuilding core services; budget vendor fees, uptime, security and switching costs.
caveat: APIs are logical interfaces, not literal physical sockets; API wrappers can still involve substantial engineering.

technical: Model-generated structured arguments indicating that a host application should invoke a specified tool.
human: A mechanic chooses a wrench from a labeled toolbox, while the shop manager still checks authorization before using it.
business: Connects assistant recommendations to verifiable workflow steps, with auditable execution.
caveat: The model doesn't execute a tool by wishing: the application must validate and run it.

technical: Retrieves relevant content from an external corpus and supplies it as context for generation.
human: An open-book exam: find the relevant pages before answering and point to where the answer came from.
business: Connects changing internal documentation without full retraining; evaluate retrieval quality and error rates.
caveat: Retrieval reduces some errors but does not eliminate fabricated or irrelevant answers.

technical: A model or system that processes or produces more than one modality of data.
human: An assistant who can read the sign, hear the voicemail, and inspect the photo—if equipped for each.
business: Turns images, voice and documents into one workflow; verify supported formats and per-modal costs.
caveat: Support varies by provider and modality.

technical: Model-specific units used to represent and process inputs and outputs; often a billing unit.
human: Taxi meter ticks rather than counting letters: the fare depends on the meter's rules and distance.
business: Estimate spend from input/output token volume, tool usage and model pricing.
caveat: Tokens are not characters and token prices are not universally negligible.

technical: A generated claim that is false, ungrounded or unsupported by available evidence.
human: A tour guide who invents a street name instead of saying they don't know, and sounds convincing.
business: Risk to trust and compliance; mitigate with retrieval, citations, checks and human review.
caveat: A fluent answer may still be incorrect, and retrieval alone is insufficient.

technical: Dense numeric representations learned so related items can be compared by distance or similarity.
human: A supermarket map that shelves 'sneakers' near 'running shoes' even when the labels use different words.
business: Can improve semantic search and discovery; measure search relevance and time-to-answer against index cost.
caveat: Similarity is not factual equivalence or guaranteed intent understanding.

technical: Updating model parameters with task-specific training examples.
human: Training a capable chef on your restaurant's house recipes—not shouting the recipe before every order.
business: Useful for repeatable style or formats at scale; compare dataset, training and maintenance cost to prompting/RAG.
caveat: Fine-tuning does not automatically add fresh facts or guarantee accuracy.

technical: Orchestrated loops of model decisions, tool execution and result checks.
human: A relay kitchen: order taker, prep cook, chef and checker pass the ticket along, with a manager for exceptions.
business: Automate multi-step operations while tracking completion, failure rates, approvals and net operating cost.
caveat: More steps introduce latency, error surfaces and governance needs.

technical: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning that trains small low-rank adapter matrices while most base weights stay frozen.
human: A tailor alters a reusable jacket with a small set of custom panels instead of weaving a whole new fabric.
business: Reduces trainable parameters and often training memory for specialization; benchmark quality and serving complexity.
caveat: Not zero-cost; some tasks need other methods and merged/adapted deployment still matters.

technical: Representing model numbers at lower numerical precision to reduce size or compute requirements.
human: Packing the same road map into a smaller suitcase: easier to carry, but some fine detail can blur.
business: May cut model memory requirements and improve deployment economics; benchmark latency, accuracy and hardware.
caveat: Lower precision can reduce quality; speedups depend on kernels and hardware.

technical: Reusing prior computation or responses instead of repeating the same work.
human: Keep yesterday's popular lunch prepped rather than chopping identical vegetables for every order.
business: May reduce latency and spend for repeat requests; monitor cache hit rates, staleness and privacy.
caveat: Caching requires careful invalidation; provider pricing differs.

technical: Technical and procedural checks that constrain inputs, tool use and outputs.
human: Seatbelts, traffic lights and driving lessons: none guarantees no crash, but each blocks a class of mistakes.
business: Protect high-cost workflows with permissions, validation, monitoring and human approvals.
caveat: Prompt-only guardrails are not a security boundary.
